data.title: Chinese new energy vehicle companies all want to become AI companies.
data.description:
Author: Beating

Chinese new energy vehicle companies now all want to be AI companies.

But this business started without algorithms or computing power, and even lacked commercial logic.

In 2009, the "Ten Cities, Thousand Vehicles" program was launched, with the government spending real money to subsidize an experimental product that no one wanted to buy. The Chinese auto industry, trapped by internal combustion engine patents for over half a century, attempted to use this opportunity to break free. Once the floodgates opened, genuine car manufacturers and rent-seeking arbitrageurs mingled, ambition and speculation racing on the same track.

Those years were rife with chaos. Some car manufacturers installed the same batch of batteries on chassis, received payment after approval, and immediately removed them to stuff into the next batch of empty shell cars to get the same approval again; some cars never even hit the road, their odometers running idle in the workshop.

Car manufacturing doesn't require understanding users; as long as you thoroughly understand financial documents, the figures submitted on paper can bring in a lot of cash. Until the list of fraudulent subsidy claimants was made public, the industry suffered a heavy blow. The public opinion around 2016 practically pronounced its death sentence; an industry nurtured by government subsidies seemed destined to perish the moment the policy phased out. But on the edge of the ruins, a real spark took root. NIO, XPeng, and Li Auto successively launched projects, with BYD, which had already invested, lying in wait. Li Bin had sold car software, He Xiaopeng had made browsers, and Li Xiang had created vertical portals. They carried the capital they had earned in the internet and mobile era, along with engineers who coded, and plunged headlong into this capital-intensive furnace that most rejected outsiders. "PPT car manufacturing" was the most prominent label thrown at them by the outside world at the time. The real turning point came in 2019. Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory was completed, and the domestically produced Model 3 entered the market at a significantly lower price. This newcomer pushed its Chinese counterparts to the brink of extinction, but it also objectively reshaped the entire electric vehicle supply chain for Chinese industry. Batteries, motors, electronic controls, and later, the crucial chips and algorithms, were forced to mature in this brutal testing ground. Riding this momentum, China's automobile production and sales have remained the world's largest for over a decade. By 2026, these companies, which had barely survived a near-death experience and finally mastered car manufacturing, suddenly didn't want to be called car companies anymore. On August 24, 2026, XPeng released its Q2 financial report. Financial websites see hundreds of these PR articles every day, and very few people bother to check the inconspicuous company profile at the end. But all the anxiety and ambition are hidden in those few lines of small print. In its 2020 IPO prospectus, XPeng described itself as a "smart electric vehicle company"; by the end of 2024, it had changed to a "global AI car company"; just a year later, it was renamed "a globally-oriented embodied intelligence company"; and by the summer of 2026, it had simply switched to the purely English title "a leading global physical AI company." Four changes in four years, the scope of its vocabulary broadened each time, but the sleazy, unsettling atmosphere faded with each passing year.

XPeng is not the only company eager to shed its traditional manufacturing label. Geely built a "full-domain AI system" at its CES booth, iterating from version 1.0 to 2.0 in two years; NIO spun off its intelligent driving chip business, attracting 2.257 billion yuan in external funding in its first round; Li Auto had already included artificial intelligence in its company-wide letter as its highest vision in early 2023, but in reality, its core profits are still firmly supported by range-extended vehicles.

The scene in the exhibition hall is also changing.

Chery replaced its sales staff who showed customers their cars with humanoid robots, whose robotic arms pointed the way to customers. Seres reclaimed control of the "Wenjie" trademark and instead created a new brand called AIVA, complete with a large external model. In the eyes of the capital market, pure hardware manufacturing has always been subject to stringent valuations. Even the most robustly welded car doors cannot escape the valuation ceiling of the manufacturing industry, making the migration to technology and algorithms a collective choice for everyone. Even those seemingly clinging to the car company brand have long since shifted their focus. Great Wall Motors' subsidiary, Haomo Zhixing, completely shut down at the end of 2025. Wei Jianjun then brought in three suppliers—Zhuoyu, Yuanrong, and Momenta—replacing the expensive early-stage approach with pragmatic supply chain procurement. BYD, with its deepest reserves, announced in early summer 2026 an investment of over 100 billion yuan, betting everything on AI, setting goals such as a zero-accident super driver and super secretary. Even Leapmotor, known for its cost control, showcased its self-developed humanoid robot at its technology day. Zhu Jiangming bluntly pointed out the essence of business: "A robot that can be used for simple tasks isn't a real skill; a robot that can make money is truly impressive." By 2026, the term "AI" had become ingrained in automakers' financial statements, organizational charts, and financing agreements. The capital market has always been stingy with hardware assembly but willing to pay a premium for cutting-edge technology. As the profits from vehicle manufacturing are rapidly diluted, no one dares to slow down at this technological transition juncture. Long Cycles and Short-Lived Companies: In 2019, NIO's stock price plummeted to just over one dollar, making Li Bin "the most miserable person that year," only recovering thanks to an investment from Hefei state-owned assets. That same year, NIO began assembling its chip team. XPeng followed closely behind. In 2020, it delivered 27,041 vehicles on the verge of collapse, its losses reaching rock bottom, and at the end of the year, it also assembled a team to develop chips. Li Auto was the slowest to act, but quietly established a chip design company in 2022. For automakers with annual sales of less than 30,000 vehicles and cash flow constantly dwindling, betting on self-developed chips is almost incomprehensible in the eyes of the traditional automotive industry. Automotive-grade chips have development cycles of several years and are extremely expensive, but the cost of purchasing chips is handing over computing power allocation, architecture, and pricing power to others. Between becoming an assembly plant and jumping into deep waters, they chose the latter. Many visionary moves in heavy industry are essentially just the only way out when forced into a corner. Another group of competitors who chose to take shortcuts paid a heavy price. In 2022, Nezha took the lead in new energy vehicle deliveries with 152,100 vehicles, with its three major production bases operating day and night and local state-owned assets vying to inject capital. Just three years later, Nezha's cash reserves were depleted, leaving it with a massive debt of 26.58 billion yuan filed by 1,631 creditors. WM Motor struggled with its restructuring plan, and HiPhi's bankruptcy plan was repeatedly postponed by the court. From annual sales champion to deep distress, only thirty-six months passed. A price war ensued. In 2023, with the reduction of subsidies, Tesla was the first to cut prices, with single-vehicle price reductions reaching up to 36,000 yuan. In early summer 2025, BYD lowered prices on 22 models, and within two weeks, more than a dozen brands followed suit. In the first five months, 73 models across the industry were offered at drastically reduced prices. In 2024 alone, 4,419 4S stores closed down nationwide. Ford's price cuts and market shake-up back then faced a rapidly expanding market; today's fierce competition is occurring in a contracting cycle. In 2025, nominal GDP growth is projected at 4.0%, mortgage balances have seen negative growth for eleven consecutive quarters, and over 60% of residents prefer savings as a safety net. The overall car market suffered a significant blow. In 2025, the total retail sales of passenger vehicles nationwide evaporated by 170 billion yuan, the average price plummeted to 170,000 yuan, ending a six-year upward trend, and the average profit margin of vehicle manufacturing fell to a historic low of 1.5%, with the average gross profit per vehicle dropping to only 14,000 yuan. In the summer of 2026, the penetration rate of new energy vehicles surged to 62.8%, but overall passenger vehicle sales in the first half of the year plummeted by 6.2%. The only growth driver was overseas sales; domestic sales declined by 20%, with exports surging by 60% year-on-year to prop up the overall situation. Subsequently, policies intervened forcefully, with regulatory authorities successively halting loss-making sales and tightening supply chain payment terms. The 15th Five-Year Plan included capacity warnings in its documents and also included a special chapter on artificial intelligence. But business logic is an objective arithmetic problem. A car company with a profit margin of only 1.5%, earning the thinnest profit in manufacturing, is expected to compete with tech giants in cutting-edge R&D for the next decade—these two figures simply don't match. Since selling cars on the ground has already reached its profit ceiling, car companies must package their accumulated engineering and algorithms and sell them a second time in a larger market. At the GTC conference in the spring of 2025, Jensen Huang broke down the evolution of artificial intelligence into four steps: perception, generation, agent, and physical AI. Physical AI, in particular, involves taking models out of the cold screen to understand gravity, friction, and stiffness in the real world, directing metal machinery to work in the unpredictable physical world. At CES the following year, he announced that the turning point for physical AI had arrived, launching the world model Cosmos, the simulation platform Omniverse, and the robotic kit Isaac. His target was a global manufacturing and logistics market worth a staggering $50 trillion. This figure is an order of magnitude larger than the annual sales of the global automotive industry. The weight of these terms directly correlates with the stature of the evangelist. As Nvidia's market capitalization crossed the $5 trillion threshold, becoming the controller of the global computing power foundation, Huang's vision quickly drew in hundreds of billions of dollars in global capital. The policies have been equally swift. From the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology listing humanoid robots as disruptive products following smartphones and new energy vehicles, to "embodied intelligence" and "artificial intelligence+" being successively included in the highest-level government work report, technical terms have rapidly gained weight in core planning for industrial layout and resource allocation. However, this cutting-edge technology is still in its pioneering stage in the industry. Li Auto, in its paper on world models published at an academic conference, frankly admitted at the outset that there is no unified definition of world models in academia. Domestic technological approaches also differ: Huawei and NIO advocate world models, while XPeng and Li Auto are betting on VLA models that integrate vision, language, and motion. XPeng publicly promotes VLA (Virtual Reality), and internal technical reports also mention teams working on world models. Momenta, dubbed the "first stock in physical AI," omitted the term entirely in its Hong Kong Stock Exchange prospectus for the sake of accuracy, listing world models only as a project under development. The technical definition is still evolving, but the concept has already been pushed to the forefront by capital. Real money is rapidly concentrating upstream along the industry chain, with the first to reap the rewards still being those who control the computing power infrastructure. Meanwhile, autonomous driving operations across the ocean present an intriguing industrial reality. Since 2024, Waymo has continuously imported over 3,000 JK chassis manufactured in China from the Port of Los Angeles. These vehicles from the Ningbo factory were cleared through customs with the autonomous driving hardware and software and network communication modules removed, entering the country as pure skateboard chassis to comply with local regulations. Upon arrival in Arizona, Magna then added the autonomous driving kits. The chassis of Waymo's driverless cars navigating the streets of the US showcases the absolute strength of Chinese manufacturing in mechanical engineering and cost control. While Chinese automakers have secured top-tier hardware orders, they still face numerous barriers in global competition regarding the algorithms and commercial operations that truly determine high-end premiums. Two benchmarks: Tesla, which has explored the deepest boundaries of technology and regulations, and Waymo, with its largest commercial operation. In early autumn of 2026, Tesla began testing passenger transport with the Cybercab, a vehicle stripped of its steering wheel, pedals, and side mirrors, showcasing a striking design. However, on the very day it hit the road, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) officially launched an investigation. The special inquiry letter directly addressed core access issues, with Inquiry Item 19 directly citing Section 135 of the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard, which explicitly states that service braking must be activated via foot controls. The test vehicle in question lacked any foot control components. Musk has yet to obtain a federal-level safety waiver. On the Texas regulatory register, Tesla's declared Cybercab fleet was updated to 45 vehicles just before its launch; in its home state of California, Tesla only holds a test license with a safety driver on the DMV list, and its name is still absent from the Utilities Commission's list of commercially operating vehicles. Even in Tesla's official reports to regulators, footnotes cautiously indicate that vehicles still require active driver supervision. From cutting-edge concept to legal commercial use, regulatory frameworks and safety redundancy remain an unavoidable hurdle. Waymo, viewed under a second benchmark, reveals the efficiency bottlenecks behind its scale expansion. As a global leader in the commercialization of autonomous driving, Waymo's weekly order volume has hovered around 500,000 for several months. Despite expanding to 15 cities and adding over a thousand vehicles to its fleet, the average weekly trips per vehicle have dropped from 167 to 125. Public calculations show that Waymo's empty-run rate in California operations remains above 40%. Its parent company, Alphabet's Other Bets segment, which includes autonomous driving, generated over $300 million in revenue per quarter, but its operating loss approached $1.8 billion. The high cost of cutting-edge exploration has not been lessened by its valuation climbing to hundreds of billions of dollars. The domestic market is also undergoing a serious technological test. In early spring 2026, multiple driverless cars were found to be out of service on elevated roads in Wuhan, triggering months of industry self-inspection and testing standard rectification. Baidu's previously optimistic profit timeline subsequently became more pragmatic, with its financial statements focusing on break-even per vehicle. Pony.ai also publicly stated that its fleet size needed to reach at least 40,000 to 50,000 vehicles for its free cash flow to turn positive, while at that time its actual operating fleet was less than 2,000 vehicles. Along the long marathon, many runners have fallen. General Motors' Cruise has slowed significantly after its accident-related restructuring, with its parent company suspending further funding; Ford-backed Argo AI announced its dissolution and wrote off $2.7 billion in assets; and Zhongzhixing ultimately went into liquidation due to a labor arbitration enforcement payment of 15,000 yuan. A startup can be tripped up by an extremely small funding gap, while the leading giants have poured hundreds of billions of yuan into this technological path, still waiting for the day when a successful commercial cycle is established. The Unshakeable Backing: Chinese automakers did not enter this industry empty-handed. In 2023, China's industrial robot density reached 470 robots per 10,000 workers, ranking among the top in the world. One out of every two newly installed industrial robots worldwide is located in Chinese factories. Four years ago, NIO, XPeng, and Li Auto all relied on external suppliers for their intelligent driving chips. Four years later, XPeng's Turing chip has shipped over 200,000 units and secured a contract with Volkswagen; NIO's Dimensity NX9031 intelligent driving chip has shipped over 550,000 units; and Li Auto's Mach M100 has delivered over 50,000 units. In terms of core hardware self-sufficiency, domestic emerging companies have truly crossed a key hurdle. However, these chips are currently all used in their self-developed closed-loop systems and have not yet been truly released as independent products to the external open market. A more complex challenge lies in the fact that, as the transition from four-wheeled cars to bipedal humanoid robots, the assets that can be directly transferred decrease progressively from the bottom up. The easiest thing to reuse is computing hardware. After its self-developed chips were successfully tested, XPeng's humanoid robots naturally inherited the same computing power; the engineering team could also collaborate horizontally. In early 2026, XPeng merged its autonomous driving center and cockpit center into a general intelligence center, with more than 200 engineers coordinating intelligent driving, robotics, and low-altitude operations. However, the closer one gets to the core of the algorithm, the more obvious the cross-domain barriers become. Cars move in planar, wheeled motion on structured roads, while humanoid robots involve full-body coordination with dozens of degrees of freedom, dynamic gravitational balance, and tactile feedback. The industry's discussion of model universality largely stays at the level of data annotation and engineering chains; specifically, the motion control algorithm still requires a completely different architecture. Even end-to-end technologies that are maturely validated in vehicles cannot be directly applied to physical robot systems. In 2024, Li Auto successfully developed and ran end-to-end intelligent driving in closed-loop development over several months. Li Xiang frankly admitted that he previously thought people working on artificial intelligence were frauds, but was completely convinced after seeing the performance of real vehicles. Li Auto attempted to replicate this development pace to the more complex VLA (Visual Language Action) model, compressing the cycle to six months. However, the generalization success rate was significantly lower than expected when deployed to complex operating conditions, forcing them to pragmatically reduce the proportion of the language model in direct control. Industry real-world testing also reflects the complexity of reality. High-order multimodal models with an order of magnitude larger parameters did not show a significant performance difference in fine-grained motion control compared to smaller, specifically optimized models. Furthermore, the completion rate of closed-loop circuits in some academic benchmark tests remains low. While the hardware is working, truly enabling a steel-bodied machine to understand the physical world remains a long and arduous scientific journey. The second wave of monetization: XPeng's Q2 2026 results reveal a new business balance. During this period, the company's automobile sales revenue reached 17.05 billion yuan, a slight increase of 1% year-on-year, with a gross profit margin of 12.1%. Meanwhile, other revenue, including technology R&D services, reached 2.7 billion yuan, a nearly 100% increase year-on-year, with a gross profit margin as high as 75.1%. On this report, the meager profit from car sales is almost equal to the high returns from technical services, creating a stark contrast between the low profit margins of traditional hardware manufacturing and the premium of software technology within the same company's accounts. However, this external extension of technological revenue generation is still in its early stages. The main external automakers actually paying for these services are Volkswagen. Volkswagen China executives have explicitly stated that Volkswagen pays for the overall electronic and electrical architecture and underlying code license, while XPeng's most differentiated core intelligent driving and cockpit applications remain independent. Outside of Volkswagen, there are few cases among OEMs capable of undertaking large-scale, complete technology licenses. Another major external revenue recorded during the same period came from carbon emission credits purchased by Porsche. The asset-heavy logic of solely selling cars is facing a ceiling, and independently capitalizing R&D results has become a common choice for automakers. XPeng's humanoid robot team, Pengxing, completed its independent spin-off and financing. Even though it has not yet entered the stage of large-scale commercialization, it still obtained a post-investment valuation of over $6.2 billion in the capital market, which is close to 60% of the market value of its parent company, XPeng Motors. NIO also spun off its self-developed chip business, Shenji, and introduced 2.257 billion yuan of external capital in its first round. Through independent financing, automakers not only isolate the cash flow pressure of their parent companies, but also find external supply channels for the long-term R&D race. As asset forms change, the pricing logic of talent is also being restructured. In early 2026, Li Auto regarded seizing the AI ​​market as a key strategy and quickly adjusted its organizational structure to establish parallel teams. In the battle for technical talent, a number of algorithm and hardware backbones went into entrepreneurship, and several AI startups that originated from automaker teams secured large amounts of financing within a few months. Li Auto subsequently participated in the early rounds of projects by former employees as a strategic investor. In the flow of capital and talent, the value scale of traditional manufacturing is being rewritten. The salary gap between manufacturing and cutting-edge software algorithms has widened to more than double, and the salary expectations of top algorithm talents are soaring. While maintaining its manufacturing base, BYD is allocating more resources to cutting-edge technology research and development; Li Auto, while controlling overall operating costs, is fully guaranteeing its core algorithm budget. The capital market treats traditional hardware and cutting-edge narratives very differently. When new car deliveries face industry price wars, the secondary market often reacts cautiously; but once it demonstrates technological depth extending to physical AI, capital tends to give a more generous valuation tolerance. BYD focuses its hundreds of billions of yuan in R&D on vehicle intelligence, Li Auto is scaling back its operations to protect its core algorithms, NIO participates in cutting-edge incubation through ecosystem investment, and XPeng is promoting the independent self-sustaining development of its technology business and robotics. Their paths differ in emphasis, but their underlying logic is the same. Given the extreme compression of profits in traditional manufacturing, automakers must learn to monetize this technological asset, forged with real money, a second time within a larger capital and commercial framework. The actual working hours of robots, failure rate, human intervention rate, and customer payback period—these four core indicators remain difficult to find in publicly available information across the industry. This is not due to deliberate concealment by companies; rather, these four sets of data are scattered deep within the actual production line, recorded in the emergency stop button trigger logs, the alarm frequency of safety light curtains, the takeover records of back-end engineers, and the cycle time sheets of the production line control system. The main manufacturers lacked long-term on-site data access rights. In the early stages of the industry, the mean time between failures (MTBF) was commonly used to represent stability. However, this metric only records the interval between two failures and cannot reflect the actual downtime losses incurred by the entire production line for each shutdown. Historically, the transition of emerging technologies and equipment from the laboratory to the workshop often requires policy mechanisms to pave the way. In the spring of 1980, Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) spearheaded the establishment of JAROL, a robot rental company, transforming expensive and uncertain robotic arms into rental equipment available on a monthly basis. Industrial policy essentially bought the first deal for the nascent market. The computing power centers scattered across various regions today, along with local state-owned asset procurement and demonstration application subsidies, are, in principle, a contemporary continuation of this model. Policies provide the platform, and enterprises test the waters, jointly offering the initial incubation ground for a potentially revolutionary cutting-edge technology. However, a significant gap remains between policy support and genuine market demand. Of the 218 winning bids in the first half of 2026, just over 20% actually resulted in orders entering the industrial production line; the remainder were mostly concentrated on prototype testing and scenario verification, with the payment cycle for some projects extended to over a year. From a financial perspective, the revenue actually earned from factory work remains relatively meager. Yushu's revenue from industrial applications is approximately 15 million yuan, accounting for less than 3% of its total humanoid robot business. Of the more than 16,000 devices shipped by UBTECH, 921 are full-size, fully-equipped intelligent robots, with the vast majority still being desktop or educational devices. Leju's revenue from industrial applications is also in the millions of yuan range. There remains a considerable technological and commercial gap between the intended orders on paper and their actual implementation in the demanding industrial environment. In contrast to the cautious approach to industrial implementation in China, customs export data reveals strong overseas demand. Starting in 2026, humanoid robots obtained exclusive customs tariff codes, with exports exceeding 10,000 units in the first seven months, totaling nearly one billion yuan. The average declared value per unit was approximately 95,000 yuan, with the largest export destination being the United States, which has the strictest supply chain audits. In late summer, Serbia launched its first European humanoid robot factory in Shabazzi, invested in by a Chinese company. Around the same time, trade and compliance barriers for related smart hardware were quietly tightening across the Pacific. The same batch of machines, equipped with algorithms and motors, faced a complex external compliance environment while simultaneously leveraging robust supply chain capabilities to enter the global market. This collective migration to new names is not unfamiliar in the history of the technology industry. More than twenty years ago, at the height of the internet boom, over a hundred publicly traded companies in the US incorporated ".com" into their names. After the tide receded, the names quickly became obsolete; what truly remained were fiber optic cables, servers, users, and cash flow. Today's physical AI will eventually undergo the same selection process. Chinese automakers have more tangible assets. Over the past decade, they have channeled massive R&D investments into factories, supply chains, chips, algorithms, and engineering teams. The question now is whether these capabilities can move beyond automobiles and into robotics, autonomous driving, and more real-world physical scenarios. Chinese automakers are betting on the next industrial revolution with the capabilities they've accumulated over the past decade. They've already won that gamble once in the past decade. From an industry that started with subsidies, was rife with fraud, and was almost universally doubted to survive, they've built the world's most complete new energy vehicle industrial system. Now, they're putting all the chips they've accumulated over the past decade onto the next table.

data.title: With industry giants entering the market one after another, why is the next battle for tokenized assets distribution?
data.description:
Author: Alea Research; Translator: Plain Language Blockchain

Coinbase, Robinhood, and Circle have recently made a series of major announcements that have a profound impact on the crypto industry. The core commonality among these projects is only one thing: asset issuance. From tokenized US stocks to stablecoins, all parties' bets this year ultimately rest on one premise—whether users can truly access and purchase these issued assets. Distribution capability is the core competitive advantage. In the 30 days ending September 10, Jumper's routing transaction volume reached $934.6 million, a 40.3% increase month-over-month; its fastest-growing target chain has only been online for 74 days.

Monthly routed transaction volume since November 2023. The recovery trend in 2026 is currently still below the peak of 2025, but the gap is narrowing.

Key Takeaways

  • LI.FI aggregates and distributes tokenized shares from xStocks, Ondo, Backpack, Robinhood, and Coinbase. Only one integration is needed to access all of the above issuers and reach over 1,000 applications and wallets. Robinhood Chain, since completing its first routing transaction on June 28th, now accounts for 7.9% of Jumper's total 30-day transaction volume, a 2.9 percentage point increase month-over-month, ranking first in growth among all target chains. The Intents mechanism allows users to use USDG on one chain and directly acquire tokenized US stocks on another chain in one step, completely eliminating manual cross-chain and exchange operations. In its first month, the Advance feature drove the median transfer amount up 39.1% to $89.42. Circle's Arc mainnet will launch on September 16th. LI.FI will provide routing support on the first day, replicating Jumper's strategy of integrating with Robinhood Chain in June. Tokenized stocks saw explosive growth in 2026. Coinbase launched its native US stock on Base in August, and LI.FI was one of the first networks to support its routing; Robinhood has built its own public chain around tokenized assets; Ondo, xStocks, and Backpack have already launched; Centrifuge signed on August 31st; Circle's Arc will open on September 16th. However, every issuer hits the same wall on launch day: if users can't successfully buy through their existing wallets, blockchains, or existing assets, then the value of on-chain stocks is meaningless. In contrast, asset issuance is a relatively easy process. This is precisely the market need that LI.FI addresses, with Jumper serving as the user front-end built on top of it. In the $5.14 billion cross-chain aggregator market, Jumper holds an 18.0% share, ranking second among 22 protocols; the top spot goes to its underlying LI.FI Routing API (23.2%). In DefiLlama's statistics, the two are counted separately as independent protocols, therefore the entire LI.FI technology stack accounts for 41.2% of the market share in this category. DefiLlama separately analyzed the two adapter sets, which together accounted for 41.2% of the market share in this category. The median transaction amount on the platform was $91, with stablecoins accounting for about half of the receiving routes. On a daily average basis, the combined daily processing volume of the two routing legs was $39.5 million, with the highest single-day volume this quarter occurring on September 4th, reaching $59.9 million. Overall growth has been steadily increasing since mid-August. Cross-chain and same-chain stacked data. Daily average reached $39.5 million over 30 days, showing a significant increase since mid-August. Robinhood Chain: Jumped from zero to 7.9% in 74 days. Robinhood Chain completed its first route on Jumper on June 28, 2026. Just 74 days later, it contributed 7.9% of Jumper's total 30-day trading volume, becoming the fifth largest target network after Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, and Solana. This equates to $73.4 million in transactions within 30 days, and a cumulative total of $119.6 million since its launch. [Image showing fund flows over two full months, with the most active day, September 8th, handling $7.79 million.] Among the target chains, Robinhood Chain saw the largest increase in share, climbing 2.9 percentage points month-over-month. Ethereum grew by 1.3 percentage points, Ink by 1.2 percentage points from a lower base, and Solana by 1.1 percentage points. No chain saw a decline of more than 1 percentage point. Overall funding is flowing to newly launched networks rather than being highly concentrated in a single leader. Robinhood Chain, Monad, and Hyperliquid occupy share ranges that were not present on the chart a year ago. Looking at the data from two dimensions—fund volume and transaction count—a starkly different picture emerges: Robinhood Chain handles nearly 26% of the daily monitored routing transactions by Jumper, but only accounts for 7.9% of the total funds. This indicates that the chain is absorbing a large amount of high-frequency, small-amount transfers, a typical characteristic of a healthy retail ecosystem. (See attached image: Robinhood Chain, viewed in green, jumped from zero in June to a quarter of the market share.) Forty Tokenized Assets and Connected Liquidity Paths The core of Robinhood Chain is tokenized US stocks, and Jumper is a crucial deposit channel. Of the 280 transaction samples that entered the chain, **52.9% arrived in ETH, and 36.1% arrived in USDG.** Each asset listed on Robinhood requires capital inflow before trading, and Jumper is the key path for delivering these funds. The Intents mechanism enables one-click direct purchase of tokenized stocks. Users can input USDG on one chain and receive SPCX directly on Robinhood Chain, where the solvers in the background conduct bidding to complete the settlement. Ethereum and USDG facilitate fund inflows, with stock trades completed once funds are received. Applications can access this link without needing to build their own complex solver networks; LI.FI has pushed it to over 1,000 integrators, including Robinhood Wallet, MetaMask, and Phantom. Jumper also operates its own website (rwa.jumper.xyz) listing approximately 40 tokenized real-world assets (RWAs), covering NVDA, SPY, gold, and short-term US Treasury bonds. Of the 120,000 routes processed by Jumper itself in the past four months, only 34 were tokenized stocks. Jumper's self-operated frontend is just one of many entry points, and it is usually the least likely to handle the final stock transactions. The core strategy is to build distribution channels in advance before real demand explodes. Securing the default channel for an asset class is the most cost-effective approach when that class is still small. ETH and stablecoins currently account for four-fifths of the assets delivered by Jumper. sUSDS has jumped to third place, accounting for 7.5%. The fragmentation of asset liquidity is far more severe than demand figures suggest, which is precisely why the intermediate infrastructure layer gains pricing power. For example, a single share of Tesla corresponds to **11 different tokens** on the LI.FI registry, scattered across **8 blockchains**, minted by multiple institutions including Coinbase, Backed, Ondo, xStocks, and Robinhood; NVIDIA also has 11 tokens. Users holding a token from one issuer cannot directly use it in venues supported by another issuer; **an intermediary protocol is required to provide unified interchangeability**.

    A single Tesla token has spawned 11 independent tokens across 8 blockchains, and the same is true for Nvidia.

    Cost Structure of Fund Flow

    Jumper launched its **Advance** feature in the first week of August: supporting simulated swaps, smart slippage, large order splitting, and providing limit order functionality through CoW Swap and 1inch. Perpetual contracts and Solana quote simulation were also added in August.

    After the feature went live, the median transfer amount rose from $64.30 to $89.42. The high-value segment showed the opposite trend: the 90th percentile amount declined by 10.8% to $2,116.34, and the proportion of large transfers exceeding $10,000 decreased from 4.2% to 3.7%. This change is primarily due to the increased density of underlying transfers. The time window required to process 1,000 transfers decreased from 2.65 hours to 1.97 hours. While the absolute number of large transfers actually increased (from approximately 380 per day to 445), their proportion in the overall market was relatively diluted due to the faster growth of smaller transfers. Four transactions exceeding $100,000 carried $1.61 million; while 569 transactions under $100 generated only $11,550. The gas cost per transaction remained relatively stable, but the relative percentage varied greatly with the amount: for transfers under $100, gas fees accounted for 0.077% of the total amount; while for transfers exceeding $10,000, this percentage was less than 0.001%. Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

OpenAI is seeking a new round of financing at a higher valuation, while also disclosing that its free cash flow will be deeply negative over the next five years, indicating significant long-term funding pressure.

On September 18, according to a recent presentation document obtained by the Financial Times, OpenAI expects to generate up to $278 billion in negative free cash flow over the next five years, primarily for large-scale expansion of computing power and infrastructure.

OpenAI projects revenue of $350 billion in 2030 and $36 billion in 2026. This represents a nearly tenfold increase in six years, with cumulative revenue from 2026 to 2030 reaching approximately $840 billion.

OpenAI projects revenue of $350 billion in 2030 and $36 billion in 2026.

Meanwhile, the parent company of ChatGPT is in talks with investors for a new round of financing, with a potential valuation of $1.2 trillion already mentioned. Sources close to the company revealed that OpenAI is pushing for a deal at an even higher valuation. This plan means OpenAI will continue to rely on external capital injections for years to come. After completing a $122 billion funding round in March, at its current rate of cash burn, the company expects to run out of funds as early as 2028, directly testing its established financial arrangements and hardware procurement contracts. High Revenue Growth Still Struggles to Offset Expenditure Pressure OpenAI's revenue prospects are not without their bright spots. Documents show that its revenue is projected to grow from $36 billion this year to $350 billion in 2030. In July, with the release of a new model, OpenAI's annualized revenue grew by approximately 20% month-over-month. It's worth noting that early forecasts in May of this year projected a five-year free cash flow deficit of $305 billion, which has since narrowed, reflecting better-than-expected commercialization progress. Despite this, OpenAI's spending far exceeds its revenue growth. The document projects that cumulative spending on computing power and infrastructure alone will reach approximately $856 billion by 2030, making it its single largest expenditure item. Competitive pressure forces price reductions, and financing needs are imminent. While OpenAI's revenue is growing, it also faces increasingly fierce market competition. To attract enterprise customers, the company has significantly reduced product pricing, needing to compete with its US rival Anthropic for market share and also contend with challenges from low-cost "open weight" models. This price war, while squeezing profit margins, further increases its reliance on external financing. OpenAI's financial situation affects a vast industry chain. According to the Financial Times, major technology groups such as Nvidia, Oracle, and SoftBank's data center business have largely staked their future revenue on contracts with OpenAI. If OpenAI's fundraising is delayed, the performance expectations of related companies will also be under pressure. In the capital market, OpenAI had previously planned to go public this fall and secretly submitted its listing application to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in June, but subsequently postponed the process, officially citing growing public concern about the risks brought about by the rapid development of artificial intelligence. However, according to some investors, there is another consideration behind the delay: internal concerns exist about whether the market can give a reasonable valuation to a company that continues to lose money. Meanwhile, competitor Anthropic is expected to go public this fall, potentially setting a record for the largest tech IPO in history, which undoubtedly adds complexity to OpenAI's search for the best time to go public.

data.title: AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google face antitrust lawsuits.
data.description:
Author: Pan Lingfei, Wall Street Insights

The regulatory controversy in the artificial intelligence industry is spreading from the policy level to the legal battlefield.

According to Politico, four plaintiffs filed a civil lawsuit last Friday in a federal court in California, accusing Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI, and Google of violating U.S. antitrust laws by engaging in illegal business collusion by publicly coordinating to slow down the development of AI. None of the four companies immediately responded to requests for comment.

The lawsuit was directly triggered by an article published earlier this month by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. The article called for "industry-wide coordination" to "control the pace of AI frontier development," which was subsequently endorsed publicly by SpaceX AI head Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis. The plaintiffs argue that this series of statements constitutes an illegal business agreement between competitors. Once this case enters the substantive trial stage, it will have a profound impact on the competitive landscape and regulatory direction of the AI ​​industry.

Core Allegation in the Lawsuit: Public Statements Deemed Illegal Coordination

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. Nick Rowley, one of the attorneys representing the plaintiffs, stated in a statement that the case aims to prevent "private, self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful for-profit technology companies" from causing AI to "rapidly escape human control."

Rowley stated, "When it comes to extinction threats such as nuclear war, and the greatest risks in human history today, humanity deserves unquestionable protection. The rule of law should be established by governments in a transparent, legal manner and accountable to the public."

The plaintiffs' legal logic is that Dario Amodei's public appeal and the responses of other industry leaders formally constitute an agreement between competitors regarding business conduct, crossing the red line of U.S. antitrust law—even if the statements are made in the name of public safety.

Plaintiff Composition: Lawyers and Ordinary Citizens Join Forces

The four plaintiffs come from diverse backgrounds.

Attorney Cheyenne Hunt, who previously participated in exposing sexual misconduct allegations against former California Congressman Eric Swalwell and former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner, has a certain public profile. The other two plaintiffs are Florida attorneys Charles Buist and Nick Spetsas, and the fourth plaintiff is California resident Christine Bullock. The lawsuit documents show that the plaintiffs intend to expand this case into a class-action lawsuit, representing all groups affected by the companies' decisions to slow down AI development. This intention means that the potential scale of claims could be significantly expanded, further increasing the case's deterrent effect on the industry. Security Controversy Sparks Calls for Slowdown The background to this lawsuit is the escalating debate in the field of AI security. It is understood that current and former AI researchers have recently issued stern warnings, arguing that without sufficient safety safeguards, the continued development of AI technology could pose a potential existential threat to human survival. The aforementioned statements from industry leaders regarding slowdowns have emerged against this backdrop. However, this lawsuit places this security discussion within an antitrust framework, creating a distinctly different legal narrative: the plaintiffs are not questioning the security risks of AI itself, but rather arguing that, regardless of motivation, coordinated actions between competitors should not be exempt from legal oversight. The plaintiffs emphasize in their complaint that the formulation of relevant rules should proceed transparently through government procedures, rather than being privately driven by companies.
